In this VladTV clip, Terrance “Gangsta” Williams breaks down prison politics, respect, and double standards behind the walls, including his view that gay inmates hold major influence at Louisiana State Penitentiary, better known as Angola. Speaking with Vlad, Williams compares street codes to jailhouse rules, discusses why “rats” are treated differently from homosexual inmates, and explains how food, jobs, and daily survival shape power inside prison. The conversation also touches on Brian “Glaze” Gibbs, the consequences of reacting violently to disrespect, and Vlad’s past interview with “Boxer,” a Mexican Mafia member who spoke about sex and violence in prison. Williams offers a blunt perspective on how fear, reputation, sexuality, and violence intersect in custody and on the streets.

In this VladTV interview, Jimmy DiModica opens up about growing up on the New Jersey side of the Gambino crime family, where mob figures at the Belmont Tavern became his early influences. DiModica discusses his father’s long criminal history, time in Atlanta Federal Prison, Jersey State Prison, and later sharing a facility with him at Otisville in upstate New York.  

From Belleville High School and high SAT scores to Newark street life and the Labor Union world, DiModica recalls how organized crime became a path to money and identity. He also talks about names tied to the Mafia era, including John Gotti, Bobby Cabot, Jimmy Palmieri, Nicky Palmieri, and Carmine Persico, plus surprising brushes with Hollywood figures like Burt Young, Robert Blake, Linda Ronstadt, and Steve McQueen.  

A raw look at Gambino family history, New Jersey Mafia culture, and true crime firsthand.

--------
In this VladTV interview, Tito “TJ” Dominguez details one of the most dramatic chapters from his 13-year federal prison sentence: a planned helicopter escape. Dominguez says the idea formed after a three-day bond hearing he viewed as unfair, leading him to buy a chopper and map out a route involving a prison pickup, sinking the aircraft in water, using a dive tank, then fleeing by car and plane to Haiti before continuing to Colombia.

He also discusses confiding in associate John Chaney, a violent figure he describes as connected to mob-style work, and how that decision allegedly backfired after Chaney began cooperating with prosecutors. Dominguez claims the story was later inflated to include false allegations about threats against a federal judge and agents, resulting in solitary confinement while he remained “under investigation.” The conversation touches on Pablo, Ramirez, Oscar, federal prison politics, cooperation, and escape planning.

--------
John Franzese Jr. sits down with Vlad to describe the fear and fallout of becoming an FBI confidential informant while surrounded by the Colombo mafia, including his father, legendary mob figure Sonny Franzese, and his brother Michael Franzese. He explains why cooperating against made men felt like a “death sentence,” especially while battling addiction, paranoia, and the constant threat of being exposed.

Franzese also recounts a 1990 gun charge that led to a year in jail, his connection to Colombo captain Ralphie Lombardi, and the destructive choices he made while drinking and using drugs. The conversation then moves to his turning point in 2001, when he says everything suddenly stopped, leading him to recovery at Odyssey House. He also shares how sobriety, a 12-step community, and a relationship that became marriage in Las Vegas helped reshape his life after the Mafia and addiction.

In this VladTV interview, Marlow Bates and Timmirror revisit their Baltimore past, the drug trade that devastated families, and the murder convictions they say were fabricated. The conversation turns deeply personal as Marlow remembers being incarcerated when his mother died, praying for God to spare her and later feeling as if God answered with “F*** you,” forcing him to confront the pain he had caused. Timmirror reflects on accountability, addiction in his own family, AIDS loss, and the prison economy—from commissary and phones to lawyers and bail bonds. They also discuss The Wire, Vlad’s memories of boarded-up blocks in Baltimore, Little Melvin, harsh crack-era sentencing, and racism in the justice system. Marlow points viewers to his Amazon Prime documentary and teases an upcoming TV series promising stories The Wire never told.

--------
Rene Enriquez sits down with Vlad to explain how parole hearings work after multiple life sentences, why concurrent terms made him eligible, and how five parole grants were reversed by California governors Jerry Brown and Gavin Newsom. After 32 years, 4 months and 11 days in prison, Enriquez describes fighting through the courts, studying reversal letters, and proving rehabilitation before his 2022 release at age 60.

The conversation also covers protective custody, cooperation in major cases, life after the California Department of Corrections, therapy for complex PTSD, nightmares about returning to prison, and the challenge of adjusting to cell phones, social media, public transportation, taxes, and everyday disrespect outside prison walls. Enriquez also discusses concerns tied to the Mexican Mafia, keeping his face blurred for safety, and why he now works to avoid violence at all costs.

--------
Former DEA agent Chris Feistl breaks down how investigators penetrated the Cali Cartel’s inner circle by recruiting Jorge Salcedo, Miguel Rodríguez Orejuela’s head of security and counterintelligence chief. In this VladTV interview, Feistl details the tense first contact in Cali, Colombia, the fear of an ambush, and the high-risk meeting that helped agents close in on Miguel after Gilberto Rodríguez Orejuela’s arrest — a storyline later depicted in Netflix’s Narcos Season 3.

Feistl explains Salcedo’s background as an Army Reserve captain, his role paying corrupt officials and protecting cartel leadership, and why he ultimately chose to cooperate with the DEA in exchange for safe passage for his family to the United States. The conversation also touches on Operation Cornerstone in Miami, the failed mercenary plot to kill Pablo Escobar, FARC, and the surveillance that narrowed Miguel’s location in the Santa Rita area of Cali.

recentItems.title: Charleston White Predicted Yella Beezy Would Be Found Guilty if He Didn't Take the Stand (Flashback)
recentItems.description:
In this flashback, Charleston White sits down with Vlad to break down the upcoming Dallas murder trial connected to Mo3’s killing, discussing prosecutors’ claims involving Kewon White, Devin Brown, Jocelyn Jackson, alleged payments, bank records, and how Yella Beezy could be tied into the case. White argues that the jury may weigh Dallas politics, Mo3’s legacy, music videos, lyrics, and courtroom testimony heavily — and says Yella Beezy may need to testify if he wants to avoid a guilty verdict.

The conversation also touches on the role of rap lyrics in court, friends allegedly mocking deaths online, Earl Spence, Hurricane Chris winning his self-defense case after taking the stand, and broader legal realities facing artists like Lil Durk amid street-related allegations. Vlad and Charleston debate whether silence helps or hurts defendants in murder cases, accountability under the law, and why fame, money, and street beef can become a dangerous mix in hip-hop.

Marlow Bates and Timmirror Stanfield sit down with VladTV to discuss life after decades behind bars, their connection to Baltimore street history, and why they say they were never paid or consulted for HBO’s The Wire. Bates reflects on serving 37 years before parole in 2022, his transition through a drug treatment program, and reconnecting with his wife and family. Stanfield opens up about coming home after roughly 40 years and adjusting to a world moving faster than expected.

--------
In this VladTV interview, John Franzese Jr. looks back on the turbulent events that led him to speak with FBI agent Rob Lewicki around 1995. Franzese describes addiction, family crisis, his mother’s threatened home, and fears surrounding his father Sonny Franzese’s parole on a decades-old case. Meeting Lewicki at Christopher Morley Park, he says he felt pressure tied to possible parole violations and rejected the idea that cooperation began simply for money.

Franzese also addresses misconceptions that he “gave up” his father, explaining what he believed was happening inside the Colombo crime family during the Orena faction conflict and later truce talks. He discusses acting as a confidential informant, refusing payment at first, conversations involving Lenny Dell, Andrew Russo, and others, and why he believed the FBI wanted insight connected to Sonny Franzese’s influence. Michael Franzese and the family fallout also loom over this candid account.

Terrance “Gangsta” Williams sits down with Vlad to discuss the difference between street violence, hits, and what the public often labels a serial killer. The conversation references Vlad’s interview with Mexican Mafia figure Ramon “Mundo” Mendoza, who described killing as a “job,” and compares that mindset with people convicted of predatory crimes in federal prison. Williams reflects on being around Mexican Mafia members, the Black Hand, and other inmates in the feds, while explaining why he doesn’t view himself in the same category as serial killers who target women or children.

Williams admits he took lives during his years in the streets and says his mindset was shaped by “kill or be killed” survival, drug dealers, and street conflicts. Now older, he acknowledges it “wasn’t right,” while still separating his past from the serial killer label. A candid VladTV discussion on crime, prison culture, morality, and accountability.

--------
In this VladTV interview, former Mexican Mafia member Rene “Boxer” Enriquez explains why he left La Eme on March 22, 2002, after decades inside the organization. Enriquez details the fear, prison politics, alleged hit lists and threats to innocent visitors that pushed him toward dropping out, then describes being separated, debriefed and flown by the FBI from Pelican Bay to Los Angeles after 9/11. He breaks down his later work with law enforcement, including Title III wiretap analysis, cooperation with the FBI, DEA, ATF and Homeland Security Investigations, and testimony in federal, state and civil cases. Enriquez also discusses his first trial in San Diego’s Southern District of California, involving Gato Marquez and Operation in the Hat, why he rejects the prison “no snitching” code, and why he refused to touch Mexican cartel cases involving family risk.
